title: Year-Round School
resolution: Resolved: Public schools in the United States should adopt a year-round calendar.
summary: Year-round schools usually keep the same number of school days but trade the long summer for shorter breaks spread through the year. Is that a better calendar?

background.p: Most year-round schools don't add days; they rearrange them. A **single-track** calendar shortens summer and adds breaks ("intersessions") through the year, in patterns like 45 days of school and 15 days off. A **multi-track** calendar splits students into groups on staggered schedules so a building can serve more students. About 3,700 public schools (4.1%) used a year-round calendar in 2011–12, according to the Congressional Research Service.

Studies of achievement are mixed and often weak in design. The CRS summarized a general consensus of no effect or a small positive effect, with some evidence of benefits for students from low-income families. Research on "summer learning loss" (for example, a review by Cooper and colleagues) found students lose ground over long summers, especially lower-income students in reading, though newer studies debate how large the loss is.

disputed.q: How large is summer learning loss?
positions: Older studies found students lose about a month of learning over the summer, more for low-income students in reading.
Some newer analyses find smaller or more varied losses and question the measurement in older studies.

terms.def: All students follow the same year-round schedule.
Students are split into groups with staggered schedules, so part of the school is always on break.
A break of a few weeks during the school year, sometimes used for extra help or enrichment.
The drop in skills some students show after a long summer break.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Shorter, more frequent breaks help students keep what they learn and give schools more ways to help.

args.claim: Shorter breaks reduce summer learning loss.
args.warrant: Skills fade without practice. A three-week break gives less time to forget than a ten-week break, so less time is spent reviewing in the fall.
args.evidence: Reviews of summer learning loss (Cooper and colleagues); district comparisons of fall review time.
args.response: The negative replies that the total time off is the same, so forgetting may simply spread across more breaks, and studies of achievement find little effect.

args.claim: It can help students from low-income families most.
args.warrant: Families with fewer resources can't always afford summer camps, trips or tutors, so long summers widen gaps. Spreading breaks and using intersessions for extra help narrows them.
args.evidence: CRS summary noting some evidence of benefits for economically disadvantaged students; research on summer reading gaps.
args.response: The negative answers that free summer programs could target those students directly without changing every family's calendar.

args.warrant: A student who falls behind in October can get catch-up help in the November intersession instead of waiting for summer school.
args.evidence: Descriptions of intersession programs in year-round districts; district reports on remediation.
args.response: The negative argues intersession programs cost money and many districts can't staff them, so the benefit depends on extra funding.

args.warrant: When a quarter of students are always on break, a building can serve more students, saving the cost of new schools.
args.evidence: CRS summary of multi-track savings, including a Clark County, Nevada study.
args.response: The negative points out that multi-track schedules put siblings on different calendars and are hard on families and staff.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Year-round calendars disrupt families and communities without clear academic gains.

args.warrant: A disruptive change should show clear benefits. Most studies find no effect or a small one, and many have design problems.
args.evidence: CRS (2014) summary of the research, including Cooper and colleagues' note that a credible study had yet to be done, and a California study finding no effect on test scores.
args.response: The affirmative replies that small gains concentrated among low-income students still matter, and weak studies mean we should try and measure, not refuse.

args.warrant: Parents must find child care for several breaks a year instead of one summer, and families with children in different schools may face different calendars.
args.evidence: CRS discussion of family scheduling problems; parent surveys in districts that tried and dropped year-round calendars.
args.response: The affirmative answers that communities adapt with intersession programs and camps, and some parents prefer breaks in other seasons.

args.claim: Summer has value of its own.
args.warrant: Summer jobs, camps, family farms and businesses, and long stretches of free time teach responsibility and independence that school can't.
args.evidence: CRS note on lost summer jobs for older students and effects on summer businesses; research on youth summer employment.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a shorter summer still leaves several weeks, and breaks in other seasons offer their own opportunities.

args.warrant: Buildings used all year need air conditioning and year-round maintenance, and staff on different schedules are harder to train and coordinate.
args.evidence: CRS discussion of higher operating costs and staff burnout concerns.
args.response: The affirmative answers that multi-track savings on buildings often outweigh operating costs, as the CRS also notes.

strawmen.strawman: They want kids in school all year with no summer at all.
strawmen.why: Most year-round calendars keep about 180 school days and a shorter summer.
strawmen.steelman: Rearranging the same number of days into shorter, more frequent breaks may reduce forgetting and allow timely extra help, especially for students from low-income families.

strawmen.strawman: They just want a long vacation.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to weak evidence, family scheduling, summer jobs and costs.
strawmen.steelman: Without clear academic gains, the costs to families, older students' summer work and school operations aren't worth the change.

weak.arg: Students in year-round school go to school more days.
weak.why: Usually false; most year-round calendars have the same number of days. The other side will catch it at once.

weak.arg: Kids will be miserable without summer.
weak.why: Students still get breaks, including a shorter summer; this overstates the change.

aff: Does your calendar add school days or rearrange them?
What evidence shows achievement gains, and how large?
neg: Is summer learning loss real for low-income students?
Would you support a year-round calendar if a district chose it?
How do families in year-round districts handle child care?

reading.title: Schools say goodbye to the long summer
Little benefit found to year-round schools
